How to think

Design Principles

These principles are not slogans. They are the rules Abyssal uses to decide where systems belong.

Build games, not demos

Features exist because Morninghollow or another real game needs them. A system should support production, not only a technical showcase.

Composition over inheritance

Actors become useful through Components, Fragments, recipes, and services. Avoid hardcoded species like UnitActor versus BuildingActor unless a real technical need appears.

Fragments define identity

A Fragment describes what an object is: its structure, default resources, tags, and visual assembly.

Runtime owns the match

Fragments may define a default Team, but explicit match context owns final team, owner, controller, lane, target, current health, and match state.

Editor builds, manual teaches

The editor should stay a workshop for creating content. The Digital Manual is the textbook for concepts, relationships, examples, and long-form explanations.

Author once, instantiate many

A saved Fragment can be placed in a Scene, spawned by a recipe, or used by either faction without duplicating asset data.

One authoritative system

Ownership follows lifetime. Assets own asset data; renderers own render state; gameplay services own runtime behavior.

Documentation is architecture

Docs explain why systems exist and how future work should fit. A feature is not complete until its responsibility is understandable.

Small stable steps

Abyssal grows by proving one layer, then building the next. Avoid broad rewrites when a narrow bridge will preserve architecture.

Architecture Notes

Color is visual presentation. Color does not determine Team. Tags can describe identity, but structured ownership should live in explicit runtime or placed-instance data.
